Microaerobic pretreatment of sewage sludge: Effect of air ﬂow rate,
pretreatment time and temperature on the aerobic process and
methane generation
S. Montalvo a, *, C. Huili~nir a, F. Ojeda a, A. Castillo a, L. Lillo a, L. Guerrero b
a Chemical Engineering Department, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Ave. Lib. Bdo. O'Higgins, 3363, Santiago de Chile, Chile
b Chemical and Environmental Engineering Department, Universidad Tecnica Federico Santa María, Valparaíso, Chile

Keywords:
Microaeration
Methane generation
Hydrolysis
Sewage sludge
a b s t r a c t
The effect of air ﬂow rate (AFR), pretreatment time, and temperature on a microaerobic pretreatment
were determined, including its effect on CH4 generation. For this, four AFR (0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 1 vvm), three
temperatures (20, 25 and 35 C) and three aeration times (24, 48 and 60 h) were evaluated in 1-L and 5-L
bioreactors. The effect on CH4 production was evaluated in 280-mL bioreactors, using previously aerated
sewage sludge. It was found that the micro-aerobic pretreatment improves the hydrolytic process, with
an increase of proteins, total sugars, soluble chemical oxygen demand (COD), and a greater removal of
volatile suspended solids (VSS) compared to a system without aeration. It was determined that an
AFR ¼ 0.3 vvm, 48 h of aeration time, and a temperature of 35 C were the best operational conditions for
increasing hydrolysis rate. VSS removal under the aerobic pretreatment follows ﬁrst order kinetics.
Finally, the aeration pretreatment allows a 211% increase of methane generation compared to a process
without pretreatment, improving also total COD and VSS removal.

1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of sewage sludge is a valuable treat-
ment that results in the reduction of sludge volume, destruction of
pathogenic organisms, stabilization of the sludge, and production
of an energy-rich biogas (Appels et al., 2008). This anaerobic
digestion involves a number of metabolic reactions including hy-
drolysis, fermentation, and methane formation. According to the
literature (Zhu et al., 2009; Abelleira-Pereira et al., 2015), the main
limiting factors of sewage sludge AD are associated with the hy-
drolysis step. Therefore, various sludge disintegration methods
have been studied as a pretreatment, where slowly degradable
particulate organic matter is converted into low molecular weight
readily biodegradable compounds, bypassing the rate-limiting hy-
drolysis stage. The pretreatments that have been reported are
physical-chemical and mechanical methods (Mata-Alvarez et al.,
2000; Divyalakshmi et al., 2015), thermo-chemical treatment
(Zhen et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2015), and biological methods (Saidu
et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Mutschlechner et al., 2015).
Among the biological methods, the use of micro-aeration as a
treatment prior to anaerobic digestion has received less attention,
even though it has been reported that the limited oxygen supply
increased the enzymatic hydrolysis rates for the case of complex
organic matter in batch tests (Johansen and Bakke, 2006). With
limited oxygen, it has been suggested that the facultative anaerobes
maintain a low redox potential and supply more growth factors for
the strict anaerobes (Gerritse et al., 1990; Kato et al., 2005). These
ﬁndings suggest that hydrolysis, and therefore COD solubilization,
might be improved by micro-aeration. Some studies about the ef-
fect of micro-aeration on anaerobic digestion have been reported,
mainly using municipal solid waste (MSW) as substrate (Charles
et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2015),
indicating that micro-aeration has an important effect in terms of
enhancing the anaerobic digestion process and this needs further
investigation. Other studies using vegetable and ﬂower wastes (Zhu
et al., 2009) and grass silage (Jagadabhi et al., 2010) have also been
carried out, indicating that the amount of oxygen supplied and the
micro-aeration time needs to be further optimized. Mshandete
et al. (2005) studied the aerobic pretreatment of sisal pulp in
mesophilic anaerobic digestion using an mixed culture of activated
sludge. They indicated that the correlation between high enzyme

activity and high methane yield using an aerobic pretreatment
suggests that such a short pretreatment period may be an alter-
native option for increasing solubilization of sisal pulp and pro-
moting methane productivity.
Regarding the effect of micro-aeration on the AD of sewage
sludge, few studies have been reported. Jenicek et al. (2011), using a
continuous bioreactor and pumping air continuously into the
sludge recirculation stream, showed that the VSS/TSS ratio of the
digested sludge, soluble COD concentration, ammonia nitrogen,
and phosphate concentration decreases in all experiments under
micro-aerobic conditions. Jenicek et al. (2010), working with a
continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) with continuous micro-
aeration, indicated that efﬁcient H2S removal, higher speciﬁc
methane production, lower methane concentration in the biogas
due to dilution with nitrogen remained from the dosage of air,
better sludge liquor quality, and lower foaming potential and foam
stability were obtained using micro-aeration. Dumas et al. (2010)
studied the efﬁciency of a hyper-thermophilic (65 C) aerobic
process coupled with a mesophilic (35 C) digester, getting a 30%
increase of COD removal and 20%e40% of biodegradability. How-
ever, the methanization yield of the process was similar to that of a
conventional process, probably due to the uptake of carbon from
the facultative biomass. Ramos and Fdz-Polanco (2013) performed
anaerobic digestion in a continuous pilot reactor in order to see the
effect of microaeration on the performance of anaerobic digestion
under overload conditions, showing that oxygen seemed to form a
more stable digestion system, which meant increased ability to deal
successfully with overloads. Therefore, none of these studies had
reported the effect of parameters such as pretreatment time,
temperature, or air ﬂow rate (AFR) on pretreatment. Also, the ki-
netics of the hydrolytic process in the aerobic pretreatment has
been scarcely reported. Knowledge of the effect of these parame-
ters on the pretreatment can help to determine an operation range
within which both pretreatment and anaerobic digestion can be
operated efﬁciently. Furthermore, the kinetics of the hydrolytic

Therefore, the goal of the present work was to determine the
effect of AFR and aeration time and temperature on the pre-
aeration process, including also its effect on the anaerobic diges-
tion process. The kinetics of VSS degradation in the pre-aeration
process was also determined.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate, inocula and experimental design
The substrate for all the assays was a mixture of primary (60%)
and secondary (40%) sludge from “La Farfana”, a municipal waste-
water treatment plant operated by Aguas Andinas in Santiago,
Chile. The inoculum had a speciﬁc methanogenic activity of 0.32 g
CH4 g1VSS d1, and it was obtained from an anaerobic reactor of La
Farfana.
Five assays were performed at the laboratory scale under the
conditions presented in Table 1. Each assay was ran on three sam-
ples of mixed sludge taken at different times, and they were run in
duplicate. The goal of assay 1 was to know the inﬂuence of the
micro-aeration pretreatment on the hydrolysis process. Assay 2 was
meant to study the effect of different pretreatment times (24, 48
and 60 h) on the solubilization of sewage sludge. This assay also
measured protein and total sugar in order to evaluate the solubi-
lization grade. Assay 3 was carried out in order to determine the
inﬂuence of temperature on hydrolysis in the microaerobic pre-
treatment. Assay 4 was run in order to determine the kinetics of
hydrolysis in the micro-aerobic pretreatment. Finally, assay 5 was
carried out to determine the effect of the micro-aerobic pretreat-
ment on CH4 generation; in this case, the contents of the aerobic
reactors were taken and put in several 280-mL anaerobic bio-
reactors (200 mL of hydrolyzed sewage sludge plus 50 mL of
inoculum), similar to the system used by Huilinir et al. (2015, 2014).
The kinetics of hydrolysis (Assay 4) was studied by the integral
method using ﬁrst order kinetics, since this is followed by the most
widely used hydrolysis model (Vavilin et al., 2008). The ﬁrst order
kinetics indicates that

2.2. Experimental setup
Assays 1, 2 and 3 were run in 1-L glass reactors, operating with
an effective volume of 900 mL. Assays 4 and 5 were ran in bigger
reactors, with a total volume of 5 L and an operational volume of
4 L. In each pretreatment, air was injected continuously into the
bioreactors by means of mini-compressors (0e10 Lpm) and
distributed by small diffusers. The air ﬂow rate (AFR) was calibrated
before the pretreatment assays using the volume variation method.
As shown in Table 1, assays 1 and 2 were carried out at room
temperature without temperature contro, while assays 3, 4 and 5
were run with temperature control.
2.3. Chemical and statistical analysis
The following parameters were determined: total COD (tCOD),
soluble COD (sCOD), total and suspended solids, volatile suspended
solids, pH, ammonia, proteins, and total sugars. COD (total and
soluble) was measured by the colorimetric method according to
(APHA et al., 2012). Total and suspended solids, volatile suspended
solids, ammonia and pH were measured according to APHA et al.
(2012). Proteins were measured by the Bradford method (Kruger,
1994), and total sugars were measured by the colorimetric
method (Dubois et al., 1956).
Methane production was measured by volumetric displace-
ment, connecting an inverted falcon tube containing a 3% w/w
NaOH solution in order to eliminate CO2 and H2S as the main im-
purities from the biogas, displacing only the methane volume. The
resulting biogas travels through the ﬂexible tubing to the Falcon
tube, where it comes in contact with the NaOH solution, forming
sodium carbonate and bubbling only methane. The methane
collected in the Falcon tube was sucked with a syringe and released
in a ﬂame to observe its presence.
The Minitab 8 software was used for the statistical processing
and analysis of the data. An ANOVA analysis was performed and a
comparison of 95% conﬁdence intervals for mean values was made.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of aeration ﬂow rate (AFR) on hydrolysis (Assay 1)
The effect of different AFR on VSS, sCOD and pH is shown in
Table 2. No signiﬁcant differences in the behavior of duplicate re-
actors in all assays were seen. Therefore, only the results of one of
the duplicate reactors will be reported. It is seen that VSS decreased

in all the assays, reaching a maximum of 37% in 2 days at vvm ¼ 0.3.
The lowest VSS decrease occurred in the anaerobic assay (without
aeration), with only 7% removal. This difference between the pro-
cess with and without pre-aeration shows that the hydrolysis un-
der the aerobic process is faster than the anaerobic one, with a
higher degree of VSS destruction (Lim and Wang, 2013). This also
accounts for the higher production of SCOD under aerobic conditions
(Table 2), due to the solubilization of the complex organic matter
(Burgess and Pletschke, 2008). In fact, the SCOD increase under
aerobic conditions varied between 26% and 85%, while it was only
10% under anaerobic conditions. This behavior agrees with the re-
sults presented by Lim and Wang (2013) and Jang et al. (2014), but it
disagrees with other reports, which show that soluble COD in pre-
aerated reactors decreases with respect to the anaerobic process
(Jenicek et al., 2011; Diak et al., 2013). This difference can be
accounted for because the pre-aerated system used here is an extra
step, where the sludge was aerated uninterruptedly during 48 h,
and after that it was digested anaerobically; in contrast, Jenicek
et al. (2011) and Diak et al. (2013) aerated the system in-situ (in
the same bioreactor and jointly with the anaerobic digestion).
Regarding pH, all the assays increased the pH value, with the
reactors with pre-aeration again undergoing a larger increase, be-
tween 3.3% and 4.07%. This pH increase can be explained by the
generation of ammonia in the hydrolysis of protein (Huilinir et al.,
2011). The pH increase does not agree with the behavior reported
by Lim and Wang (2013), who showed that pH decreased during
the pre-aeration step (4 days). In our case, the presence of a high
nitrogen content in the sludge allows an increase in pH and better
operational conditions for the anaerobic step.
It should be pointed out that from 24 h after the beginning of the
assays, H2S concentration in the liquid phase was undetectable.
This behavior is expected because of the oxidation of sulfur by
sulfur-oxidizing biomass, a situation also reported in other studies
(Krayzelova et al., 2014). Furthermore, the oxygen concentration in
all the assays also had values lower than the lowest limit of the
sensor, showing that the conditions in the assays correspond to a
micro-aerobic system.
Therefore, from these results it can be stated that pre-aeration
allows increasing the hydrolysis process, with an AFR ¼ 0.3 vvm
as the best option in order to increase the hydrolysis rate of com-
plex organic matter.
3.2. Effect of aeration time on protein and carbohydrates hydrolysis
(Assay 2)
Assay 2 was used to determine the effect of different pre-
aeration times on the process at 0.3 vvm. The effect was seen in
the protein and total sugar behavior, also including total ammonia
nitrogen (TAN). Fig. 1A shows that the soluble protein concentra-
tion increased with respect to the anaerobic test. The largest in-
crease (341%) was achieved at 48 h, while the lowest (42%) occurred
at 60 h. This behavior can be accounted for by the hydrolysis of
particulate proteins, which release amino acids and ammonia
(Fig. 1C). The increase can also be accounted for because a part of
the mixed sewage sludge coming from an activated sludge process
(40%) developed ﬂocs in order to improve the decantation. These
ﬂocs can release the soluble protein in the liquid phase, a process
called “deﬂocculation”, and it is attributed mainly to a low aeration
in the activated sludge process. This was exactly what happened in
the pre-aeration treatment, so this can also explain the larger
production of soluble protein (Morgan-Sagastume and Allen,
2005).
Fig.1B shows the total sugar concentrations at different aeration
times, and it is seen that longer aeration times increase the soluble
sugars in the liquid phase, with increases up to 300% at 60 h. Since it
is known that hydrolysis is the rate-limiting step for carbohydrate
conversion (Miron et al., 2000), the results show that the pre-
aeration improves carbohydrate hydrolysis, allowing better solu-
bilization for further anaerobic processes. Fig. 1B also shows that
the difference between the soluble sugars obtained at 48 h and 60 h
is small, so the improvement of carbohydrate hydrolysis is marginal
when aeration time increases from 48 h to 60 h.

Fig. 1C shows the total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) concentration
obtained at different pretreatment times. It is seen that aeration
time increases the release of ammonia in the liquid phase mainly
because of protein hydrolysis. The same asa in assay 1. this increase
also accounts for the pH increase in the media. In this assay pH
increases from 5.6 to 6.4, a situation that also favors the further
anaerobic process. It is important to note that ammonia nitrogen
concentration does not rise to inhibitory values for anaerobic
digestion, varying between 1500 and 3000 mg TAN L1 (Chen et al.,
2008; Montalvo et al., 2014), although at times it has been possible
to acclimatise anaerobic systems at as much as 4000 mg L1 of TAN
(Gao et al., 2015).
All earlier results show that a pre-aeration time of 48 h is
enough to increase the hydrolysis of proteins and carbohydrates.
3.3. Effect of temperature on aerobic hydrolysis (Assay 3)
The effect of temperature on the microaeration pretreatment
was studied in assay 3. The results of soluble COD are given in
Table 3, where it is seen that a temperature increase causes
increased soluble COD production, reaching as much as 85% at a
temperature of 35 C. This shows that the hydrolysis was favored at
higher temperatures, even though the solubility of oxygen de-
creases. As mentioned by Luo et al. (2012), the increase of soluble
organic matter at higher temperatures is due mainly to a hydrolytic
process, because the particles obtained have higher kinetic energy
and facilitate enzymeesubstrate interactions, thereby increasing
the hydrolysis rate.
The effect of temperature on VSS degradation was also studied,
and the results are shown in Table 4. The same as for soluble COD,
VSS solubilization increases at higher temperatures, with a 42%in-
crease at 35 C. These results agree with the study of Komemoto
et al. (2009), who show that the solubilization of complex organic
matter (food waste) increases in a mesophilic temperature range.
This also accounts for the greater presence of soluble CODs at 35 C.
Therefore, according to these results it is clear that mesophilic
temperatures allow good performance of aeration pretreatment.
3.4. Kinetics of the hydrolysis of VSS under aerobic pretreatment
(Assay 4)
Once the effect of AFR, aeration time, and temperature were
evaluated, the kinetics of hydrolysis under microaerobic conditions
was studied at 25 C and 35 C. The experimental and model results
are shown in Fig. 2, where it is seen that in both experiments the
behavior of VSS solubilization follows ﬁrst order kinetics, with
values of R2 greater than 0.95. First order kinetics has been estab-
lished in several reports as a good model to represents the hydro-
lysis under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions (Vavilin et al.,
2008; Batstone et al., 2010). It is also seen that solubilization was
faster at 35 C, as mentioned earlier, with values of 0.226 d1 and
0.269 d1 for k at 25 C and 35 C, which are in the range reported in
the literature for anaerobic hydrolysis (Vavilin et al., 2008), and
they also agree with reports that state that even though hydrolysis
under aerobic conditions is faster, enzymatic activity under aerobic
and anaerobic conditions is not different (Goel et al., 1998).
3.5. Effect of micro-aerobic pretreatment on organic matter
removal and methane generation in an anaerobic process (Assay 5)
The effect of aeration pretreatment on methane generation and
organic matter removal was studied in assay 5, which was per-
formed with sewage sludge pretreated at 35 C and 0.3 vvm for
48 h, and the results are presented in Figs. 3 and 4. Regarding total
COD (Fig. 3A), it is seen that its total removal in the process with
pre-aeration is 80%, while without aeration it is only 57%. This
situation clearly shows that a pretreatment allows greater total
COD removal, almost twice as great when the aeration pre-
treatment was applied. It should be mentioned that the original
total COD of mixed sludge before aeration was 134.077 g L1, with a
total removal of 84% with the pre-aeration anaerobic digestion in

Fig. 3B gives the results for soluble COD, showing that the trend
in both reactors was similar, with an increase of soluble COD con-
centration until day 16, followed by its decrease. This trend was also
found by Diak et al. (2013) using primary sludge pre-treated with
micro-aeration. The soluble COD increase during the ﬁrst 16 days
can be attributed to the hydrolytic process, which generates soluble
COD that later will be used in the methanogenesis (Burgess and
Pletschke, 2008). The soluble COD increase was slightly greater in
the pre-treated sludge, with 4% increase with respect to the values
obtained with the raw sludge. After 16 days, soluble COD in both
cases starts decreasing, with this decrease more signiﬁcant in the
anaerobic process of pretreated sludge. This behavior shows that
the pre-treatment improves not only the hydrolytic step of anaer-
obic digestion, but also the methanogenesis process.
Fig. 3C shows the effect of the pre-aeration step on VSS degra-
dation under anaerobic conditions. The proﬁle was similar to that
obtained for total COD, with greater VSS removal in the process
with pre-aeration. Without pre-aeration, VSS degradation was only
33%, while with pre-aeration it was 68%, or twice as large. Fig. 3C
also shows that VSS removal was faster during the ﬁrst 16 days,
coinciding with the increase of soluble COD in the liquid phases.
The greater removal obtained in the process with pre-aeration can
be attributed to the solubilization of slow biodegradable organic
matter in the aerobic step, thereby increasing the total removal of
VSS. Greater VS removal in aerobically pretreated wastes was also
reported by Xu et al. (2014), who worked with food waste, ﬁnding
that hydrolysis in pretreated systems varied between 66.3% and
78.1%, showing improvement compared to the control (61.2%).
The greater removal of total COD, soluble COD and VSS was also
reﬂected in higher methane generation in the anaerobic treatment
with pre-aerated mixed sludge as seen in Fig. 4, which shows that
the methane accumulated in the process with pre-aeration was
211% greater than that obtained in the process without pre-
aeration. It should be noted that this increase is greater than
those achieved using other pretreatments. For instance, increases
between 20% and 79% have been reported with mechanical pre-
treatment, between 20% and 85.9% with thermal pretreatment, and
between 20% and 112% with biological pretreatment (Harris and
McCabe, 2015).
The methane volumes obtained in both assays are in the range
of values reported in other studies. Huilinir et al. (2015), using
sewage sludge from the paper and pulp industry, obtained close to
225 mL of CH4 per gram of VSadded, and Xu et al. (2014) also ob-
tained values of 270 mL of CH4 per gram of VSadded. The higher
methane production in the system with pretreated sludge agrees
with that of other studies. Diaz et al. (2011) showed that aeration
reduces the time required to reach maximum methane production,

as well as its volume, in the anaerobic digestion of cellulose. Ramos
and Fdz-Polanco (2013) also showed that micro-aeration contrib-
utes to increase the biogas quality in a continuous system. Xu et al.
(2014) also found an increase (between 5% and 18%) in methane
generation in reactors with food waste pretreated aerobically.
Thus, it is shown that pre-aeration can be used as pretreatment
for increasing solubility, methane yield, and VSS removal in a batch
system.
4. Conclusions
Pretreatment of controlled microaeration improves the hydro-
lytic process, with increased protein, total sugars, and soluble COD,
and a greater removal of VSS compared to a system without aera-
tion. It was determined that an air ﬂow rate of 0.3 vvm, a 48-h
aeration period, and a temperature of 35 C were the best opera-
tional conditions for increasing the hydrolysis rate. The kinetics of
VSS removal in the aerobic pretreatment follows ﬁrst order ki-
netics, with values of k ranging between 0.226 d1 and 0.269 d1.
The aeration pretreatment allows a 211% increase in methane
generation with respect to a process without pretreatment,
improving also total COD and VSS removal.
